newsitem.title: UK: Palmoil price seen falling but set for soft landing.
newsitem.headline: Palmoil price seen falling but set for soft landing.

text.p: The price of palm oil needs to fall to regain its competitive position in the vegetable oil market but it seems set for a fairly soft landing in coming weeks, traders said.

"We are not going to see anything dramatic happen on the palm oil market but once people have seen the Malaysian Palm Oil Registration and Licensing Authority (PORLA) figures at the weekend we may get some idea where we go from here," said one trader.
Most European traders agree palm oil is over-priced against soft oils, but they dispute the timing of any price fall or even whether it will happen at all.
"February is always a low production month owing to the holidays in the Far East and we are going to see speculators playing on this for a while, but it can't last for ever," said one trader.
"I think the market still has some upside in it, but it will soon top out,' said another.
Some traders said Indonesia may hold the key to the market.

"At the moment the Indonesians are holding local prices down and are likely to do so until their election in March. This may make some people, who up until now have been bullish, give up on the market," said a trader.
Others said some players were tired of the market and had taken their profits and not been seen since.
Traders said Pakistan had been expected to return to the market but so far has not made a move.
"Prices in Pakistan are high and their stocks are low, so they should be making an appearance but they have not been seen yet,' said one.
Prices are still too high for China even after its recent cut in palm oil import duty.
"China still cannot afford palm oil and while prices stay at their current level we won't see any major buying from them," said another trader.
Traders said it could be the middle of next week before any trend is seen.
"A lot of people in Malaysia are still on holiday and won't return until Monday, which will slow the market down," said one trader
"We need to see what PORLA has to say at the weekend and get some idea of the export situation next week, also hear what whispers are coming out of the plantations on production," the trader added.
